lesson.title: Riding Into Danger: The Freedom Riders of 1961
lesson.summary: In 1961, interracial groups of activists rode buses through the segregated South to test enforcement of Supreme Court rulings desegregating interstate travel, facing mob violence, including a firebombing near Anniston, Alabama, before federal action finally forced compliance.
lesson.body:
By 1961, the Supreme Court had already ruled, twice, that segregation on interstate buses and in the terminals that served them was unconstitutional. Morgan v. Virginia in 1946 addressed seating on the buses themselves, and Boynton v. Virginia in 1960 extended that ruling to the waiting rooms, restrooms, and lunch counters inside interstate bus terminals. Both rulings, however, were routinely ignored across much of the South, with little enforcement to back them up. The Congress of Racial Equality, led by James Farmer, decided to test whether the law would actually be enforced by organizing interracial groups of volunteers to ride buses together through the Deep South, sitting together regardless of race and using terminal facilities together, and see what happened.

The first Freedom Ride left Washington, D.C., on May 4, 1961, with riders traveling on regularly scheduled Greyhound and Trailways buses toward New Orleans. The ride passed through the Upper South with only scattered incidents, but on May 14, 1961, a mob attacked a Greyhound bus outside Anniston, Alabama, slashing its tires and then firebombing the bus once it stopped. The riders escaped the burning vehicle only to be beaten by the surrounding mob. A separate group of riders on a Trailways bus was also badly beaten that same day, first in Anniston and again after arriving in Birmingham, where local police, under the authority of Commissioner Eugene Bull Connor, were notably absent from the terminal when the attack began, having reportedly given local Klan members time to assault the riders before intervening.

The violence nearly ended the rides. The original riders, injured and unable to find a bus driver willing to carry them further, considered stopping in Birmingham. Student activists from Nashville, including Diane Nash, argued that abandoning the rides after a violent attack would prove that violence could defeat the movement, and organized a new group, many of them affiliated with the recently formed Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, to continue the ride from Birmingham toward Montgomery. There, on May 20, 1961, another mob attacked riders arriving at the bus station, beating several severely, including John Lewis and a white rider named Jim Zwerg, while local police again were slow to respond. The violence finally prompted federal action: United States Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy sent federal marshals to protect the riders and pressed Alabama's governor to restore order.

The rides continued into Mississippi, where authorities avoided further mob violence but instead arrested riders en masse for violating segregation ordinances by using whites only facilities, sending many of them to serve weeks in the maximum security Mississippi State Penitentiary at Parchman Farm. Rather than deter further rides, the arrests and continued national press coverage drew hundreds more volunteers to join Freedom Rides throughout the summer of 1961. Sustained pressure on the Kennedy administration eventually produced concrete results: in September 1961, the Interstate Commerce Commission, at the Justice Department's urging, issued new regulations with real enforcement power, requiring the desegregation of interstate bus and train terminals, effective November 1, 1961. What two Supreme Court rulings had failed to achieve in practice, the Freedom Riders achieved through direct action, sustained organizing, and a willingness to accept real physical danger to force the government's hand.
